> How much are the licensing/exam fees generally?

Well for my state, there's:

  • $20 application fee (non-refundable)

  • $750 for first category license and $250 for additional category licenses.

  • $100 per examination category

  • $500 for initial licensing

  • $500 annual license renewal (per license)

  • Oh and a $100 abeyance fee (if your license gets suspended)

...its a lot, but its less than student loans!

> How much does hiring a PI generally cost?

PIs are generally self-employed and create their own rates.

I think the lowest per-hour model is $25ph, while the average may be $75-150ph. Other PIs may not use billable hours and instead have a day plan, where the lowest may be $100 per day. Also its common practice for customers to cover expenses, including equipment maintenance and traveling.

I don't know how much I'll be going for :P

It depends on my financial situation when I'm finally licensed; most of my billings will probably go to keeping the business afloat (meeting that $500 annual fee) and paying off a percentage of student loans. I don't feel very fat-catty atm.

How do you go about becoming a PI? Is some sort of licence/training required for it? Do PIs have any tools available to them that a normal "civilian" doesn't have?

How do you go about becoming a PI? Is some sort of licence/training required for it?

Yes, but it depends upon the state. However the general guidelines are:

  • Be of eighteen years of age or older.

  • Undergo a background check by licensing board and/or FBI.

  • Have 2-4 years of experience in law enforcement, security, or similar

OR

  • Have a degree in Criminal Justice, Criminology, Police Science, etc + 1-3 years of relevant work experience.

  • Pass licensing exam + exam fee.

  • Pay licensing fee.

I'm almost ready to begin taking the exam; I'm currently finishing up the second year of my CJ degree. Most states require an associates degree (2 years), but I'm going for a bachelors degree. My bachelors will reward me with 1 & 1/2 years of "credit", or basically I get to work less as an officer, security, bouncer, etc to be eligible for a license. Work credit needed in my state is 3 years, so that's half of my required work hours just by educating myself :)

Also I didn't mention this, but you can be licensed in more than one state if you'd like, but only serious investigators making lots of money can afford it. You have to re-exam for whatever state you're getting licensed in, testing on their laws, and have to pay a fee towards their board. I'm probably not going to do this, not unless I pull in some associates and create an agency...

Do PIs have any tools available to them that a normal "civilian" doesn't have?

Kind of... its not really tools ... you can't pick-lock homes, that's illegal... and there isn't exactly a national crime database that you gain access to upon licensing, but the license does afford a PI some advantages:

  • PIs are able to engage a business to conduct investigations on things such as all employees, certain employees, efficiency, background checks, look through confidential records, etc.

  • Provide expert testimony.

  • Locate records (which is all so much easier with confidential access!).

  • Or any of the 101 items listed on the great Diligentia Blog!

Just a bit of personal info, but Diligentia Blog and Pursuit Mag are my two most favorite PI resources. Not only are they informing, they provide relevant entertainment and PI humor.
